EPIC: External integrations for alerting, ticketing and documentation publishing

<!-- synapse-epic:external-integrations:v1 -->

## Why this EPIC

Synapse finds, verifies and reports security issues, but almost none of that reaches the tools where teams work. A new critical finding, a breached SLA, a pending approval, an expiring risk acceptance or a finished DAST run stays inside the console until someone opens it. There is no Jira handoff, no Confluence page, no Teams or Telegram channel, and no per-person routing.

This EPIC closes the gap end to end: event producers, delivery, message content with default and custom templates, channels, ticketing, documentation publishing, per-user routing, inbound webhooks and the admin UI.

Priority: the notification and integration flows come first. Every alert must reach chat, email, pager and ticketing with a sensible built-in template, and a tenant must be able to replace that template with its own wording without a code change.

- Code audit of `main` at `09f9a927` (2026-09-25). Every claim below cites the file that backs it.
- An architecture, security and fact-check review of the first draft. Its findings are folded into this text.

## Goal

Migrate **Power Exchange & Roles** into Catalog V2 without flattening orientation, named dynamics, style, and relationship structure into one peer list.

Parent V2 issue: #255  
Completed prior batches: #256–#261  
Deferred R&P batch: #262  
M16 parent: #124

This is a design/migration batch only. Do not mutate runtime canonical data.

## Canonical Power Exchange & Roles corpus

- Dominance
- Submission
- Master/slave dynamic
- Owner/property dynamic
- Daddy/babygirl dynamic
- Mommy/little dynamic
- Caretaker/little dynamic
- Pet/Owner dynamic
- Handler/pet dynamic
- Total power exchange fantasy
- 24/7 power exchange
- Weekend / temporary TPE
- Switching
- Bratting
- Brat taming
- Training dynamic
- Ownership ritual
- Protective dominance
- Gentle dominance

- Devotional submission

Relevant modern staged additions:
- Financial domination / findom
- Algorithmic / system authority
- related digital/financial/control concepts in neighboring categories

## First-pass conceptual layers

### 1. Core orientation / role preference
Candidates:
- **Dominance**
- **Submission**
- **Switching**

These appear independently rateable and foundational.

Open question:
Should Switching remain standalone, or be represented as explicit preference for both Dominance and Submission plus a switching identity/mode?

### 2. Named dynamic / relationship structure
Candidate families:
- Master/slave
- Owner/property
- Caregiver/little
- Pet/Owner or Handler/Pet
- Training dynamic
- Total Power Exchange

These should be evaluated using the standard Item test:
> Would someone independently rate this named dynamic, and would collapsing it into generic Dominance/Submission lose meaningful identity?

### 3. Style / flavor refinements
Likely refinements rather than standalone Items:

**Dominance styles**
- protective
- gentle / soft
- possibly disciplinary
- possibly service-oriented / nurturing where validated

**Submission styles**
- soft / affectionate
- disciplined / accountability-focused
- devotional

These should remain explicitly rateable refinements where useful.

### 4. Scope / temporal structure
Likely refinements of Power Exchange / TPE rather than standalone Items:
- scene-only
- ongoing
- 24/7
- temporary / weekend
- other bounded durations

Avoid creating separate Items solely for duration/scope.

### Dominance
**Standalone Item.**

Potential refinements:
- style: protective, gentle, disciplinary, etc.
- scope/context where useful
- relationship framing where not better represented by another named dynamic

### Submission
**Standalone Item.**

Potential refinements:
- style: soft/affectionate, disciplined, devotional
- scope/context where useful

**Likely standalone Item**, because enjoyment of role-switching itself may be meaningful beyond independently liking Dominance and Submission.

### Owner/property dynamic

- Daddy / babygirl
- Mommy / little
- Caretaker / little

Orphan sweep liveness keys on discovery.lock, which nothing in-tree writes and NEAT-AI spells .discovery.lock (src/discovery_cleanup.rs::is_directory_orphaned)

<!-- finding-id: SEC-bbe3f392d7aa -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-706 -->

The orphan sweep's only liveness signal is a file named `discovery.lock`
(`discovery_cleanup.rs::LOCK_FILE_NAME`), but **no production code in this
crate writes it**, and the one known host — NEAT-AI — writes
**`.discovery.lock`** (leading dot) into each session directory. A host that
calls the FFI `clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs` on NEAT-AI's `.discovery/`
root therefore reads every live session as orphaned and deletes it with its
in-flight data. Severity low (NEAT-AI does not bind the FFI sweep today, so no
live path), confidence high (both names verified, deletion reproduced).

Found by the chunk 11 security sweep, Issue #2234 (tracker #2095).

## Why this matters

- `discovery_cleanup.rs::is_directory_orphaned` treats a directory as
  abandoned exactly when `<dir>/discovery.lock` is absent;
  `clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs_since` then removes every such directory
  older than the scan start.
- `LOCK_FILE_NAME` has no in-tree production writer — only tests create it.
  The contract lives in the caller: `docs/FFI_API.md` § "Orphaned Directory
  Sweep" and the doc comment on `ffi/utilities.rs::clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs`
  say a subdirectory "is considered orphaned when it has no
  `discovery.lock` file".
- NEAT-AI `src/discovery/DiscoveryCleanup.ts` declares
  `const LOCK_FILE_NAME = ".discovery.lock"` and writes it from
  `createDiscoveryLockFile`. The two names never match, so the ownership
  signal the sweep relies on is unenforced: nothing in either repo checks

Reproduced against the current tree: a `.discovery/<uuid>/` holding only
`.discovery.lock` is swept with `removed: 1` and the directory is gone.

## Attacker model

No attacker needed — this is an integrity/availability defect triggered by
ordinary host behaviour. The trigger is a host (today's NEAT-AI, or a future
refactor that adopts the Rust sweep in place of its TypeScript one) invoking
the FFI sweep on a root its own sessions populate.

## Trigger

`clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs({"baseDir": ".discovery"})` while NEAT-AI
sessions are running under `.discovery/<creature-uuid>/`.

## Exploit sketch

1. NEAT-AI starts a discovery session: `.discovery/<uuid>/` with
   `.discovery.lock` inside, data being written.
2. Any caller runs the FFI sweep on `.discovery`.
3. `is_directory_orphaned` probes `discovery.lock` → `NotFound` → orphaned;
   the directory predates the scan, so the age floor passes it; the #1903
   re-check probes the same wrong name and passes it too.
4. `fs::remove_dir_all` deletes the live session's recording.

## Suggested fix

Make the sweep fail closed on either spelling: treat a directory as in use
when `discovery.lock` **or** `.discovery.lock` is present (in
`is_directory_orphaned`, and in the `assert_is_discovery_dir` contents
check), document both in `docs/FFI_API.md`, and note the host's spelling
beside `LOCK_FILE_NAME`. The fix ships
`tests/issue_2256_orphan_sweep_host_lock_name.rs`, which **fails before the
fix**: a `.discovery/<uuid>/` holding only `.discovery.lock` must survive
`clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs` (the session directory is the canary) with
`removed == 0`.

message_tool_only: stranded-reply recovery re-prompts the model to publish its private final and force-sends an English error notice to the DM (no config to disable)

## Summary

In `message_tool_only` mode (`messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`), a turn that ends with a **private** final text and no `message(action=send)` is classified as a "stranded reply". The recovery then:

1. **re-prompts the model with the private text verbatim** and tells it to deliver it: *"Your previous reply was not delivered … Your reply text was: "<finalText>" … Please deliver this reply now by calling message(action=send). Do not add any extra commentary; just deliver the original reply."*
2. if the retry sends nothing, **delivers a runtime notice** to the chat — `I generated a reply but could not deliver it to this chat. Please try again.` — marked `isError` + `deliverDespiteSourceReplySuppression`, so no reply mode can hold it back.

This defeats the main reason to pick `message_tool` in a customer-facing DM: keeping the model's final text private. The code says `message_tool_only` "keeps normal final text private by design" (comment on `warnPrivateMessageToolFinal`), but recovery actively tries to publish that text, and there's no config key to turn it off.

## Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.6**, Linux, Telegram DM
- `messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`, `messages.groupChat.visibleReplies: "automatic"`
- Support agent answering end customers. Private finals are internal notes ("handled, nothing else to do; context: …"), and they can mention other conversations.

## Why we use `message_tool`

With the default `automatic` mode, the agent answered the customer via `message(action=send)` and then wrote an internal note as its final text. That note went out as a second Telegram message about 3 s later. We saw 8 such leaks in about 10 turns. Switching to `message_tool` fixed that: `final reply suppressed by sourceReplyDeliveryMode: message_tool_only … deliverDespiteSuppression=false` shows up in the debug log exactly as expected.

## Reproduction (live, Telegram DM)

1. Send a DM that makes the model end a turn with a long (≥280 chars) final text and no `message` call. In our case this was a duplicate of an already-answered request, and the model wrote itself a 937-char note summarising what it had done.
2. Gateway log: `final reply suppressed by sourceReplyDeliveryMode: message_tool_only … textChars=937 deliverDespiteSuppression=false`. This part is correct.
3. Right after that, `resolveStrandedReplyRecovery` returns `kind: "retry"`. A follow-up run is injected with the prompt above, which contains the full private note, and with `toolsAllow: ["message"]`.
4. Our model **refused**, because the note referenced other customers' cases. A more compliant model would have sent the internal note to the customer. That is the leak `message_tool` is supposed to prevent.
5. The retry sent nothing, so `kind: "diagnostic"` delivered `I generated a reply but could not deliver it to this chat. Please try again.` to the customer DM, in English, although the conversation was in Polish.

Source: `src/auto-reply/reply/stranded-reply-recovery.ts` (`resolveStrandedReplyRecovery`, `buildStrandedReplyRetryPrompt`, `buildStrandedReplyDeliveryFailurePayload`). Compose: config set MYSQL_PASSWORD breaks the instance; no way to rotate the database password

On Compose, there is no supported way to rotate the bundled database's root password, and the obvious attempt breaks the wiki.

`canasta config set MYSQL_PASSWORD=<new>` updates `.env` (and `vars.yaml` on gitops instances), then restarts. But the `db` service only reads `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=${MYSQL_PASSWORD}` when it initializes an empty data directory. On an existing volume, the account in MariaDB keeps the old password, so after the restart:

- the web container can no longer connect to the database
- the `db` healthcheck (`mariadb-admin ping -u root -p$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`) fails

K8s already blocks this key in `config set` and prints a rotation procedure (`roles/config/tasks/_validate_key.yml`). Compose accepts it and silently produces a broken instance.

Rotating this credential is routine after any suspected exposure. For example, an RCE in a bundled extension (such as CVE-2026-100382 in ExternalData) exposes the web container's environment, which includes `MYSQL_PASSWORD`.

## Expected

On Compose with the bundled database (`USE_EXTERNAL_DB=false`), `config set MYSQL_PASSWORD=<new>` should:

1. Run `ALTER USER` for `root@'%'` and `root@'localhost'` in the running `db` container, authenticating with the current password and passing the new one outside argv and logs.
2. Only then write `.env` and `vars.yaml` and restart.

Alternatively, a dedicated command could do the same. Either way, `WIKI_DB_PASSWORD` needs the same handling when `--wikidbuser` is not root.

With an external database, `config set` should refuse, or warn that the password must be changed on the database server first.

Carry pfSense conversion skips into F-1 findings, not just a report parameter

Filed from #302's review (@SamikaPerera). Not started -- this is the scope stub, deliberately kept out of #302 itself.

## The gap #302 does not close

#302 fixed the *disclosure* half of a real problem: a skip note from `pfsense_convert.py` (a rule it could not model) used to reach the user exactly once, at upload, and be gone by the time a report was downloaded later. That's fixed -- the downloaded report now carries the skip list and its coverage statement stops claiming "nothing was skipped" when something was.

It does not fix the *modelling* half. Skipping a `pass` rule makes the emitted Cisco ACL stricter than the real device. A policy rule asserting "this traffic must be denied" can then report `status="none"` (clean) against the emitted ACL, while the real firewall actually permits that traffic -- a genuine policy violation, reported as a pass. See `CLAUDE.md` section 7's "UPDATE, 6 September" entry for the full direction analysis (skipping a `block` rule is the safe, noisy direction; skipping a `pass` rule is the dangerous, silent one).

## The more complete fix

Carry each conversion skip into the F-1 findings list itself, as a `status="error"` card -- which is what it actually is: "part of this config could not be checked." That would:

- Show up on the dashboard directly, not only in a downloaded report.
- Be counted by `analysis/coverage.py` the same way any other blind spot is, rather than needing a second, parallel `conversion_gaps` parameter (which #302 added as the smaller, faster fix).
- Let a reader connect a specific skip to the specific policy rule it might be silently affecting, if the finding names the interface/rule clearly enough.

## Why this needs its own scoping, not a bolt-on to #302

- **Which check owns it?** A conversion skip isn't produced by `access_control`, `policy_compliance`, or `routing` -- it's a property of the source file, discovered before the pipeline ever runs a check. Needs an id prefix decision (not `PC-`/`AC-`/`RT-`/`CH-`/`CV-` -- another collision the team has cared about avoiding, most recently for #239's `cve_mapping`).
- **Where does it enter the pipeline?** `analysis/pfsense_convert.py`'s skip list is produced by `web/main.py`'s upload handler, before `analysis.pipeline.analyse()` is ever called. Getting it into the findings list means either widening `analyse()`'s signature (an F-3 shared-contract question) or injecting it after the fact in `web/main.py` the way `_attach_explanations()` already injects a key -- but a NEW finding is a bigger change than a new key on an existing one.
- **Does it apply beyond pfSense?** Today only `pfsense_convert.py` produces a skip list. If Cisco IOS parsing (via Batfish) can also silently drop something, the same mechanism should probably cover it too, which needs checking rather than assuming.

## Acceptance criteria (draft, not final -- needs a design pass first)

- [ ] Decide the id prefix and which module owns emitting these findings.
- [ ] Decide how the skip list reaches `analyse()`/the pipeline without widening `run(bf)`'s signature for every other check.
- [ ] A skipped rule appears as a `status="error"` finding on the dashboard, not only in a downloaded report.
- [ ] `analysis/coverage.py`'s `conversion_gaps` parameter (added in #302) is retired once this lands, since the findings list itself would carry the same information.
- [ ] Full suite green, mutation-tested the same as #302's own two guards.

## 1. Resumen

La idea del proyecto es armar un sistema de detección de intrusiones (NIDS) basado en Machine Learning. El sistema recibe los datos de un flujo de red (protocolo, servicio, duración, bytes y paquetes enviados en cada sentido, TTL, etc.) y decide si ese flujo es tráfico normal o un ataque. Como segunda tarea, también intentamos predecir de qué tipo de ataque se trata.

Para esto usamos el dataset UNSW-NB15 con la división en train y test que publicaron sus autores. Vamos a comparar una regla simple sin IA y una regresión logística contra XGBoost, validar con cross-validation sobre el train y evaluar el modelo final una sola vez sobre el test. Al final queremos tener un pipeline reproducible y un script de consola que reciba un CSV con flujos y devuelva las predicciones.

## 2. Definición del problema

Los IDS tradicionales funcionan con firmas, es decir, reglas escritas a mano para ataques ya conocidos, y les cuesta detectar variantes nuevas. Nuestra propuesta es entrenar un modelo que aprenda cómo se comporta el tráfico malicioso a partir de ejemplos etiquetados, para que funcione como una capa más de detección.

Planteamos dos tareas sobre los mismos datos:

- **Binaria (tarea principal):** normal o ataque.
- **Multiclase (tarea secundaria):** Normal o una de las 9 categorías de ataque del dataset (Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, Exploits, Fuzzers, Generic, Reconnaissance, Shellcode y Worms).

### PEAS

| | |
|---|---|
| Performance | Tarea binaria: recall de ataques y tasa de falsos positivos, además de F1 y PR-AUC. Tarea multiclase: Macro-F1 y F1 por clase. |
| Environment | Registros de flujos de red del dataset UNSW-NB15. Es un entorno parcialmente observable porque solo tenemos los metadatos del flujo y no el contenido de los paquetes. Es estático, ya que trabajamos sobre archivos CSV. |
| Actuators | Para cada flujo, el sistema devuelve una etiqueta (normal/ataque o categoría de ataque) junto con su probabilidad. |
| Sensors | Las 42 variables que trae cada registro: protocolo, servicio, estado de la conexión, duración, bytes y paquetes por sentido, TTL, pérdidas, jitter, tiempos del handshake TCP, tamaño medio de los paquetes y contadores de conexiones recientes. |

Usamos UNSW-NB15, un dataset armado por el Australian Centre for Cyber Security de UNSW Canberra (Moustafa y Slay, 2015). Lo descargamos desde la página oficial (research.unsw.edu.au/projects/unsw-nb15-dataset). Trabajamos solamente con la partición en train y test que publicaron los autores:

- `UNSW_NB15_training-set.csv`: 175.341 registros.
